title: BRICKSTORM_Backdoor_Investigation_518
description: Investigate and respond to the BRICKSTORM backdoor malware compromise in the target network.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target network has been compromised by a sophisticated backdoor malware named BRICKSTORM. This malware uses advanced techniques to evade detection, including SOCKS proxying, multi-layered web service communication, and varied command execution. Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident. Learning objective: Gain practical experience in identifying and analyzing malicious services, persistence mechanisms, and processes in a compromised Unix/Linux environment. The flags you will be looking for include service names, file paths, and process names.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target host with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target host's IP address is `192.168.50.5`. To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start' in the provided input field.
levels.local_content: Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario. To proceed to the next level, enter the word 'start' in the provided input field.

levels.title: Identify Suspicious Service
levels.content: Identify and investigate an unauthorized or suspicious service running on the target host. The flag is the name of the suspicious service.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any services that seem unusual or unauthorized. The suspicious service in this scenario is named `lab-checkin.service`. The flag is the name of the suspicious service. Analyze the service details to confirm its suspicious nature. Use the `systemctl status lab-checkin.service` and `journalctl -u lab-checkin.service` commands to analyze the service details.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by understanding the concept of services in a Unix/Linux environment.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Consider how you would list all running services on a Unix/Linux system.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services.

hints.title: Advanced Command Hint
hints.content: To filter the output and make it easier to analyze, you can use the `grep` command to search for specific patterns in the service names or descriptions.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot. The flag is the path to the systemd service unit file.
levels.solution: To determine the persistence mechanism, investigate systemd services and timers. The suspicious service `lab-checkin.service` is configured to start automatically using a systemd service unit file located at `/etc/systemd/system/lab-checkin.service`. The flag is the path to the systemd service unit file. Use the `cat /etc/systemd/system/lab-checkin.service` command to view the contents of the service unit file and analyze its configuration.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand the concept of persistence mechanisms in Unix/Linux environments.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Consider how systemd services and timers can be used to maintain persistence.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Check the systemd service unit files in `/etc/systemd/system/` for the suspicious service.

hints.title: Advanced Command Hint
hints.content: Use the `systemctl cat` command followed by the service name to display the contents of the service unit file.

levels.title: Identify Suspicious Process
levels.content: Identify the process responsible for suspicious activity on the host. The flag is the name of the suspicious process.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious process, analyze running processes and correlate them with network connections. The process responsible for the suspicious activity is named `netcat-openbsd`. The flag is the name of the suspicious process. Use the `ps aux | grep netcat-openbsd` command to list all running processes and the `netstat -tuln | grep netcat-openbsd` command to list network connections. Correlate the process with suspicious network activity.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand the concept of processes and their relationship with network connections.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Consider how you would list all running processes and network connections on a Unix/Linux system.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use the `ps aux | grep netcat-openbsd` command to list all running processes and the `netstat -tuln | grep netcat-openbsd` command to list network connections.

hints.title: Advanced Command Hint
hints.content: To filter the output and make it easier to analyze, you can use the `grep` command to search for specific patterns in the process names or network connections.
